tests.name: 01_allies
tests.label: and_gates/01_allies
tests.description: Pure AND gate test. Two independent facts must both hold. Tests Psi_and factor with two premises and role swapping (x,y) and (y,x).
tests.document: Jack trusts Jill. Jill trusts Jack. If two people trust each other, they are allies.
tests.question: Are Jack and Jill allies?
tests.lexicon_raw:
predicate trust {agent: e, patient: e}
  "to have confidence in someone"

predicate allied {agent: e, patient: e}
  "to be in alliance with"

entity jack : e
  "a person named Jack"

entity jill : e
  "a person named Jill"
tests.facts_raw:
trust(agent: jack, patient: jill)
trust(agent: jill, patient: jack)
always [x:e, y:e]: trust(agent: x, patient: y) & trust(agent: y, patient: x) -> allied(agent: x, patient: y)

tests.name: 02_one_sided
tests.label: and_gates/02_one_sided
tests.description: AND gate negative test. Only one direction of trust present. Verifies AND gate correctly blocks when one premise is missing.
tests.document: Jack trusts Jill. If two people trust each other, they are allies.
tests.question: Are Jack and Jill allies?
tests.facts_raw:
person(theme: jack)
person(theme: jill)
trust(agent: jack, patient: jill)
rarely [x:e, y:e]: person(theme: x) & person(theme: y) -> allied(agent: x, patient: y)
always [x:e, y:e]: trust(agent: x, patient: y) & trust(agent: y, patient: x) -> allied(agent: x, patient: y)

tests.name: 03_dating
tests.label: and_gates/03_dating
tests.description: AND gate with different predicate. Same structure as allies but using likes/dating vocabulary. Confirms AND gate is not predicate-specific.
tests.document: Jack likes Jill. Jill likes Jack. If two people like each other, they are dating.
tests.question: Are Jack and Jill dating?
tests.lexicon_raw:
predicate like {agent: e, patient: e}
  "to find pleasant or attractive"

predicate dating {agent: e, patient: e}
  "to be in a romantic relationship with"

entity jack : e
  "a person named Jack"

entity jill : e
  "a person named Jill"
tests.facts_raw:
like(agent: jack, patient: jill)
like(agent: jill, patient: jack)
always [x:e, y:e]: like(agent: x, patient: y) & like(agent: y, patient: x) -> dating(agent: x, patient: y)

tests.name: 01_ambitious
tests.label: and_plus_depth/01_ambitious
tests.description: AND gate plus depth. Rule 1 infers henry is successful. Rule 2 combines loves(mary,henry) with inferred type(henry,successful) through AND gate. Tests mixing evidence and inferred premises.
tests.document: Henry is king of France. Mary loves Henry. If a man is king of a country, he is successful. If a girl loves a successful man, she is ambitious.
tests.question: Is Mary ambitious?
tests.facts_raw:
man(theme: henry)
girl(theme: mary)
king_of(theme: henry, reference: france)
country(theme: france)
love(agent: mary, patient: henry)
always [x:e, c:e]: man(theme: x) & king_of(theme: x, reference: c) & country(theme: c) -> successful(theme: x)
always [x:e, y:e]: girl(theme: x) & love(agent: x, patient: y) & successful(theme: y) -> ambitious(theme: x)

tests.name: 02_powerful
tests.label: and_plus_depth/02_powerful
tests.description: Three-premise AND gate plus depth. Rule 1 has three premises (old, king_of, large country) -> powerful. Rule 2 has two premises (loves, powerful) -> ambitious. Tests larger AND gates and two-level inference chain.
tests.document: Henry is old. Henry is king of France. France is a large country. If an old king rules a large country, he is powerful. If a girl loves a powerful king, she is ambitious. Mary loves Henry.
tests.question: Is Mary ambitious?
tests.facts_raw:
old(theme: henry)
king_of(theme: henry, reference: france)
country(theme: france)
large(theme: france)
girl(theme: mary)
love(agent: mary, patient: henry)
always [x:e, c:e]: old(theme: x) & king_of(theme: x, reference: c) & country(theme: c) & large(theme: c) -> powerful(theme: x)
always [x:e, y:e]: girl(theme: x) & love(agent: x, patient: y) & powerful(theme: y) -> ambitious(theme: x)

throw(agent: john, patient: rock1, target: window1)

always [w:e, o:e]: broken(theme: w) & owner_of(theme: o, reference: w) -> upset(theme: o)

tests.name: 02_domino
tests.label: causation/02_domino
tests.description: Long causal chain. Four-step domino effect. Tests forward propagation through event-triggered rules. Similar to depth chains but with causal rather than type semantics.
tests.document: Pushing domino A knocks over domino B. Pushing domino B knocks over domino C. Pushing domino C knocks over domino D. Someone pushed domino A.
tests.question: Is domino D knocked over?
tests.lexicon_raw:
predicate push {patient: e}
  "to apply force to move something"

predicate knocked_over {theme: e}
  "toppled or fallen over"

entity a : e
  "domino A"

entity b : e
  "domino B"

entity c : e
  "domino C"

entity d : e
  "domino D"
tests.facts_raw:
push(patient: a)
always: push(patient: a) -> knocked_over(theme: b)
always: knocked_over(theme: b) -> knocked_over(theme: c)
always: knocked_over(theme: c) -> knocked_over(theme: d)

tests.name: 01_if_rains
tests.label: conditionals/01_if_rains
tests.description: Causal chain through conditionals. Rain -> wet ground -> slippery road. Tests forward chaining through multiple single-premise rules with non-type predicates.
tests.document: If it rains, the ground gets wet. If the ground is wet, the road is slippery. It is raining.
tests.question: Is the ground wet?
tests.facts_raw:
raining()
always: raining() -> wet(theme: ground)

tests.name: 02_missed_bus
tests.label: conditionals/02_missed_bus
tests.description: Causal chain with future modality. Miss bus -> late -> boss angry. Tests forward inference with implicit future tense and possessive in conclusion.
tests.document: If you miss the bus, you will be late. If you are late, your boss will be angry. Tom missed the bus.
tests.question: Will Tom's boss be angry?
tests.facts_raw:
boss_of(theme: boss1, reference: tom)
miss_bus(theme: tom)
always [x:e]: miss_bus(theme: x) -> late(theme: x)
always [x:e, b:e]: late(theme: x) & boss_of(theme: b, reference: x) -> angry(theme: b)

tests.name: 01_not_mortal
tests.label: contrapositive/01_not_mortal
tests.description: Contrapositive reasoning. If all men are mortal and Zeus is not mortal, Zeus is not a man. Tests backward reasoning from negated conclusion.
tests.document: All men are mortal. Zeus is not mortal.
tests.question: Is Zeus a man?
tests.facts_raw:
not mortal(theme: zeus)
always [x:e]: man(theme: x) -> mortal(theme: x)

tests.name: 01_two_children
tests.label: counting/01_two_children
tests.description: Simple counting via conjunction. Has son AND has daughter -> has two children. Not real counting — just AND gate matching specific pattern. Tests whether structured counting can reduce to logic.
tests.document: Alice has a son named Bob. Alice has a daughter named Carol. If someone has a son and a daughter, they have two children.
tests.question: Does Alice have two children?
tests.lexicon_raw:
predicate son_of {theme: e, reference: e}
  "to be a male child of"

predicate daughter_of {theme: e, reference: e}
  "to be a female child of"

predicate has_two_children {theme: e}
  "to have exactly two children"

entity alice : e
  "a person named Alice"

entity bob : e
  "a person named Bob"

entity carol : e
  "a person named Carol"
tests.facts_raw:
son_of(theme: bob, reference: alice)
daughter_of(theme: carol, reference: alice)
always [x:e, s:e, d:e]: son_of(theme: s, reference: x) & daughter_of(theme: d, reference: x) -> has_two_children(theme: x)

tests.name: 01_devoted
tests.label: degree/01_devoted
tests.description: Degree modification on verb. "Really loves" vs "loves" distinguished by degree role (high). Rule only fires for high-degree love. Tests degree as a role dimension on predicates.

entity high : e

man(theme: henry)
love(agent: mary, patient: henry, degree: high)
always [x:e, y:e]: girl(theme: x) & love(agent: x, patient: y, degree: high) & man(theme: y) -> devoted(theme: x)

tests.name: 01_socrates
tests.label: depth_chains/01_socrates
tests.description: Basic depth chain. Single-premise rule. Type entailment: man -> mortal. Minimal test that inference works at all.
tests.document: Socrates is a man. All men are mortal.
tests.question: Is Socrates mortal?
tests.facts_raw:
man(theme: socrates)
always [x:e]: man(theme: x) -> mortal(theme: x)

tests.name: 02_poodle
tests.label: depth_chains/02_poodle
tests.description: Four-link depth chain. Tests belief propagation across multiple hops. poodle -> dog -> animal -> living thing.
tests.document: Bob is a poodle. All poodles are dogs. All dogs are animals. All animals are living things.
tests.question: Is Fluffy an animal?
tests.facts_raw:
poodle(theme: fluffy)
always [x:e]: poodle(theme: x) -> dog(theme: x)
always [x:e]: dog(theme: x) -> animal(theme: x)

tests.name: 03_food_chain
tests.label: depth_chains/03_food_chain
tests.description: Four-link depth chain with indefinite noun phrase. Tests Skolem introduction for "a sparrow" and chain: bird -> animal -> organism -> mortal.
tests.document: A sparrow is a bird. All birds are animals. All animals are organisms. All organisms are mortal.
tests.question: Is a sparrow mortal?
tests.facts_raw:
bird(theme: sparrow1)
always [x:e]: bird(theme: x) -> animal(theme: x)
always [x:e]: animal(theme: x) -> organism(theme: x)
always [x:e]: organism(theme: x) -> mortal(theme: x)

tests.name: 01_lonely_or_exciting
tests.label: disjunction/01_lonely_or_exciting
tests.description: Disjunction in premise. Either condition suffices. Tests noisy-OR — multiple independent causes for same conclusion.
tests.document: Jack is lonely. If someone is lonely or exciting, people like them.
tests.question: Is Alice lonely?

lives_alone(theme: alice)
always [x:e]: lives_alone(theme: x) -> lonely(theme: x)
always [x:e]: lives_alone(theme: x) -> finds_exciting(theme: x)

tests.name: 02_either_parent
tests.label: disjunction/02_either_parent
tests.description: Disjunction with two separate rules that conclude the same thing. Mother -> parent and father -> parent. Tests noisy-OR combining.

predicate father_of {agent: e, patient: e}

  "a person named Bob"

tests.name: 01_if_rich
tests.label: hypothetical/01_if_rich
tests.description: Counterfactual. The conditional is hypothetical and the premise is false. Tests that hypothetical modality blocks inference when antecedent is negated.
tests.document: If John were rich, he would buy a house. John is not rich.
tests.question: Will John buy a house?
tests.facts_raw:
person(theme: john)
not rich(theme: john)
rarely [x:e]: person(theme: x) -> buy_house(theme: x)
always [x:e]: rich(theme: x) -> buy_house(theme: x)

tests.name: 02_would_win
tests.label: hypothetical/02_would_win
tests.description: Conditional with satisfied antecedent. Unlike the counterfactual, this premise is true. Tests that conditional fires when antecedent holds. Contrasts with hypothetical/01.
tests.document: If the team practices every day, they will win the championship. The team practices every day.
tests.question: Will the team win the championship?
tests.facts_raw:
practice_daily(theme: team1)
always [x:e]: practice_daily(theme: x) -> win_championship(theme: x)

tests.name: 01_clark_kent
tests.label: identity/01_clark_kent
tests.description: Identity/coreference. Two names for same entity. Tests that properties transfer through identity relation. Classic intensionality test case.
tests.document: Clark Kent is Superman. Superman can fly.
tests.question: Can Clark Kent fly?

predicate identity {theme: e, reference: e}
  "to be the same person as"

predicate can_fly {theme: e}
  "able to fly through the air"

entity clark : e
  "Clark Kent"

entity superman : e
  "Superman"
tests.facts_raw:
identity(theme: clark, reference: superman)
can_fly(theme: superman)
always [x:e, y:e]: identity(theme: x, reference: y) & can_fly(theme: y) -> can_fly(theme: x)

predicate largest_city_in {theme: e, reference: e}
  "to be the largest city in"

entity paris : e
  "the city of Paris"

entity france : e

capital_of(theme: paris, reference: france)
largest_city_in(theme: paris, reference: france)

tests.name: 01_careful
tests.label: modality/01_careful

tests.question: Should Mary be careful?

man(theme: guy1)
love(agent: mary, patient: guy1)
in_class(theme: mary, reference: class1)
in_class(theme: guy1, reference: class1)

tests.name: 02_umbrella
tests.label: modality/02_umbrella

tests.question: Should you bring an umbrella?
tests.facts_raw:
raining()
always: raining() -> should(content: bring_umbrella())

tests.name: 01_popular
tests.label: multiple_rules/01_popular
